title: Baby Planet Found! It's Less Than 1 Million Years Old
summary:
Imagine a baby that is only one day old. Now imagine a baby planet that is less than 1 million years old. That sounds old, but in space time, it's a newborn! Astronomers just found the youngest planet ever seen. It's called Elias 2-24 b.

This baby planet is still wrapped in the gas and dust that made it. It orbits a young star about 450 light-years from Earth. That's very far away, but telescopes can still see it. The planet is about as big as Jupiter, the largest planet in our solar system.

How did they find it? They used a special tool called a coronagraph. It blocks the bright light of a star so we can see faint things nearby. The planet was hiding in a gap in the dust around the star. "The planets should be found within the gaps, since they are carving them," said Andrea Bernardi, a scientist who led the study. "And that's exactly where we found Elias 2-24 b."

This is a big deal because most planets we know are billions of years old. They are fully grown. This one is still forming! It's like catching a cake while it's still baking in the oven.

Scientists are excited because this baby planet doesn't fit their models. They thought big planets take about 5 million years to form. But this one formed much faster. "Elias 2-24 b shows us that even our best planet-formation models are still missing some important processes," said Lucas Cieza, a co-author of the study.

So what's next? Scientists will keep watching this baby planet. They want to learn how planets are born. Maybe one day we'll understand how our own Earth was made!
why_it_matters: Learning how baby planets form helps scientists understand how our own Earth was made, which is exactly the kind of big question you might ask in science class one day.

background_read: Our own solar system formed about 4.6 billion years ago, so planets usually take a very, very long time to grow.
A light-year is the huge distance light covers in one year, so 450 light-years is far, far away — yet telescopes can still spot things that far off.
Scientists found the first planets outside our solar system in the 1990s, and since then they have kept finding more, including this newborn one.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers led by Andrea Bernardi, with co-author Lucas Cieza, studying a young star far from Earth.
WHAT: They found the youngest planet ever seen, Elias 2-24 b, still wrapped in the gas and dust that made it.
WHERE: In a gap in the dust around a young star about 450 light-years from Earth.
WHY: The planet formed faster than scientists' models predicted, so it could teach us how planets — and our own Earth — are born.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled to catch a planet while it is still forming, because that almost never happens.
They may say one planet is not enough proof; scientists need to find more like it before they change their models.
It shows there is still a lot left to discover about how planets are born.
